title: Before the Storm
subtitle: The plans, forces and criminal orders behind the opening assault
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: On the eve of invasion, Germany had prepared to destroy the Soviet armies near the frontier. It had not solved the larger problem of defeating a state capable of continuing the war.
body:
An invasion assembled in the dark

On the evening of 21 June 1941, the German army’s eastern deployment had become an enormous exercise in concealment whose purpose was almost exhausted. The headquarters, bridging equipment, ammunition columns and attacking formations were in position for an operation that would begin before the following morning was fully light. Across the frontier, Soviet commanders were receiving warnings without receiving an equally clear political permission to act on all their implications. The German situation sheet for that evening shows the imbalance particularly well: an attacker arranged for a specific operation faced a defender whose considerable forces were still passing from peacetime organization into wartime deployment. The map records a German assessment, compiled into an atlas in 1942; its neat symbols should not be mistaken for equally complete knowledge on either side of the frontier. [1] The invasion was not simply a larger repetition of the campaign in Poland. Its commanders hoped to reproduce the operational successes of 1939 and 1940, but they were applying those methods to a much greater territory and to a state whose capacity to replace lost armies they seriously underestimated. Simultaneously, the regime had prepared a war in which military conquest, political destruction, racial persecution and economic exploitation would reinforce one another. The central contradiction was already present before a shot was fired: Germany was preparing a campaign whose political ambitions were almost unlimited while relying on military arrangements that required a rapid decision. [2] This study begins with that contradiction because it explains much of what follows. A panzer formation’s movement on a map was a real military achievement; it was not proof that the Soviet state was approaching its last reserves. A Soviet division’s presence near the frontier was a real deployment; it was not proof that the division was supplied, informed or ready to fight as part of a coherent front. On 21 June, both governments possessed imposing inventories. The decisive differences concerned what those inventories could actually do in the next hours and what their leaders imagined a war would demand. For the inhabitants of the borderlands, even the word “frontier” concealed a recent history of violence. Eastern Poland had been invaded and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1939; Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia had been occupied and annexed in 1940. The German attack would cross a boundary created by coercion and conquest, not an uncontested line between settled national communities. That history belongs to the atlas’s Poland studies. Here its immediate significance is that millions of people were about to encounter another invading power, carrying its own prescriptions for who could live, who should work and who should disappear. [2]

From cooperation to a war of conquest

The German–Soviet arrangements of 1939 had made the partition of Poland possible and helped both dictatorships pursue their immediate objectives. They had not reconciled Hitler to the continued existence of the Soviet Union. After the defeat of France, Germany’s inability to bring Britain to terms sharpened his search for a decisive continental solution. Destroying the Soviet state promised, in his calculation, to remove a potential British partner, secure resources and open the east to German domination. Strategic calculation and ideological purpose therefore converged; one did not merely provide a respectable cover for the other. The German planning record places the development of this offensive in 1940, well before the immediate border alarms of June 1941. [3] That chronology matters to the later German claim of a preventive war. Soviet military thinking included offensive operations, and Soviet deployments were not those of a government indifferent to the possibility of war. Neither fact establishes that Germany’s attack was an emergency response to an imminent Soviet invasion. Hitler’s directive of 18 December 1940 instructed the armed forces to prepare to defeat the Soviet Union while the war against Britain continued. It also required subordinate orders to disguise those preparations as precautions against a possible change in Soviet behaviour. The document’s internal distinction between purpose and explanation is unusually revealing: the attack was being prepared; its concealment would invoke a hypothetical Soviet threat. [4] There was no single moment when all cooperation stopped and all hostility began. Trade, diplomacy and operational preparation could proceed simultaneously. Stalin sought to postpone a confrontation while improving the Soviet military position; Hitler could accept economic deliveries while assembling the force intended to destroy the delivering state. Interpreting the continued relationship as evidence of mutual confidence misses the coercive and instrumental character of the arrangement. It also exaggerates Stalin’s freedom to control its ending: avoiding an incident could reduce one pretext for war, but it could not cancel an invasion already chosen for broader reasons. [3] [2] The geographical consequences of the 1939–40 expansion were similarly double-edged. Soviet power had moved westward, adding strategic depth between the old border and major cities. Yet the Red Army now had to garrison unfamiliar territory, construct new defensive works and adapt roads, depots and communications to a longer forward position. The army did not receive the full military value of the additional territory merely by occupying it. A buffer could become a trap if formations were committed near its outer edge without the preparation needed to withdraw or counterattack coherently. This was particularly dangerous around the Białystok salient, where the frontier projected westward between German starting positions. [2]

What Directive 21 actually required

The first objective in Directive 21 was the destruction of the main Soviet forces in the western part of the country. German armoured thrusts were to prevent organized armies from retreating into the interior. Territorial advance mattered because it could produce that destruction and deprive surviving forces of bases; it was not supposed to substitute indefinitely for a decisive military result. The directive’s ultimate line, conventionally rendered as the Volga–Archangel line, expressed the intended scale of domination. It should not be read as the destination of a single uninterrupted tank movement, still less as a line the Germans expected to reach during the first eighteen days. [4] The planning process also contained unresolved questions about priorities after the initial battles. Moscow was the central railway and political objective favoured by much of the army leadership. Hitler attached enormous importance to Leningrad, the Baltic region and the resources of Ukraine. The scheme north of the Pripet Marshes contemplated defeating the Soviet forces in Belarus and facilitating the destruction of those in the Baltic region before completing later advances. To reduce this to three independent races for three cities is to erase the intended interaction between the army groups and the disputes over what should happen once the frontier armies were beaten. [3] The date often extracted from the directive, 15 May 1941, referred to completing preparations that required substantial advance work. It was not an unconditional promise that the invasion would begin that morning. Subsequent changes, including the Balkan campaign and the practical problems of concentration, affected the eventual opening. Those developments deserve consideration, but a claim that every German failure in the east resulted from a fixed number of “lost” weeks assumes the very quick victory that needs to be demonstrated. The operational problem was not simply how much summer remained. It was whether German forces could destroy the Soviet capacity to continue before their own system of supply and replacement became inadequate. [4]

Reading the order

A preparation date is not a city deadline

The directive’s 15 May requirement concerned readiness for the operation. It does not establish that Minsk, Smolensk or Moscow had to fall on a particular day in June or July. Later studies compare events with specific orders where those exist, and with operational objectives where they do not. This prevents an attractive but misleading calendar of invented German deadlines. [4]

German confidence rested partly on recent experience. In Poland and France, the disruption of communications and the encirclement of major formations had produced consequences far beyond the immediate point of penetration. There was good reason to expect those methods to cause another military catastrophe. There was much less reason to assume that the Soviet state would be unable to raise additional forces after such a catastrophe. The plan depended on a judgment about an enemy society and its institutions, not merely on the speed or quality of German tanks. In that judgment, intelligence limitations and racial contempt operated together.

Three army groups and four mobile striking forces

Army Group North, commanded by Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb, assembled in East Prussia. Georg von Küchler’s Eighteenth Army and Ernst Busch’s Sixteenth Army supplied the principal infantry formations, while Erich Hoepner’s Fourth Panzer Group provided the mobile striking force. Their immediate theatre was Lithuania and Latvia, with crossings of the Western Dvina—Daugava in Latvia—essential to the continuation towards Pskov and Leningrad. The infantry and mobile forces had related but different jobs: a leading formation might secure a bridge while the following armies defeated bypassed resistance, widened the corridor and protected the route over which its supplies would have to pass. [2] Army Group Center, under Fedor von Bock, possessed the concentration most capable of producing a deep double envelopment. Hermann Hoth’s Third Panzer Group would strike from the northern side of the Białystok salient; Heinz Guderian’s Second Panzer Group would operate from the south, across the Bug in the Brest sector. Adolf Strauss’s Ninth Army and Günther von Kluge’s Fourth Army would attack between and behind them. Minsk lay beyond the salient, on the route towards the Berezina, the upper Dnieper and Smolensk. The two armoured groups gave Bock a capacity that neither neighbouring army group possessed in the same form: he could drive two major mobile arms around a concentration of Soviet forces rather than ask one arm to create the entire encirclement. [3] Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South faced a different problem. Ewald von Kleist’s First Panzer Group, Walter von Reichenau’s Sixth Army and Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s Seventeenth Army would attack into western Ukraine. Farther south, Eugen Ritter von Schobert’s Eleventh Army and Romanian forces would operate from Romania. The northern striking force had to negotiate rivers, roads and Soviet concentrations while maintaining contact with infantry and protecting an exposed flank towards the Pripet region. The southern wing was initially assigned a more restricted role; a large offensive from the Prut would begin only in July. Treating the whole army group as if it crossed one starting line and advanced at one speed conceals those differences. [3] The German air forces were organized to support this operational design. Luftflotten 1, 2 and 4 supported the northern, central and southern sectors respectively, while retaining their own command arrangements. Their opening tasks included attacks on Soviet aviation and communications as well as direct support for the ground advance. Air superiority could isolate formations, disrupt a counterattack and make daylight movement exceptionally dangerous. It could not occupy a railway junction, repair a bridge or deliver all the fuel required by a panzer group. The partnership between aircraft and mobile ground forces was powerful precisely because their functions were complementary, not interchangeable. [2]

An army in the middle of becoming another army

Opposite these concentrations stood the western Soviet military districts. On the Baltic approaches, Fyodor Kuznetsov commanded the Baltic Special Military District, which would become the Northwestern Front. Dmitry Pavlov commanded the Western Special Military District, the basis of the Western Front. Mikhail Kirponos’s Kiev Special Military District would become the Southwestern Front. Markian Popov’s Leningrad district covered the northern approaches, while the southern command arrangements were being reorganized around forces in the Odessa district and a new Southern Front headquarters. A “front” in Soviet usage was a large operational command, broadly comparable to a German army group, rather than simply the line where soldiers were fighting. [2] The Soviet forces were substantial, but their organization was undergoing rapid expansion and repeated reconstruction. Mechanized corps were being created on a scale that outstripped the immediate supply of trained personnel, transport, maintenance facilities and communications equipment. The establishment of a headquarters and the assignment of tanks did not instantly create a force capable of moving, fuelling and fighting together. Jacob Kipp’s study of the covering forces is useful here because it distinguishes the intended role of the forward armies from the incomplete arrangements through which they had to perform it. They were supposed to protect mobilization and concentration while responding to an attack; in practice, German operations would begin disrupting those very processes before they were completed. [5] The T-34 and KV tanks illustrate the difference between a weapon and a functioning formation. Their armour and armament could confront German units with serious tactical problems, as the first week would show. Yet a tank required a trained crew, suitable ammunition, fuel, recovery equipment, orders and information about neighbouring units. Numbers that aggregate new vehicles, older machines and equipment awaiting repair cannot by themselves explain how many tanks a commander could employ at a particular crossing. Nor does the later reputation of the T-34 establish that every formation receiving it in June 1941 could exploit its advantages immediately. [2] The same caution applies to the effects of Stalin’s purges. The removal, imprisonment and killing of officers damaged the armed forces and encouraged a climate in which an incorrect judgment could become a political charge. But “the purges” cannot explain every broken radio, unfinished deployment or failed movement order. Expansion itself created a shortage of experienced officers; new organizations required new skills; recent reforms had not finished working through the army. These causes interacted. A rapidly promoted commander attempting to master an unfamiliar formation was doing so inside a political system that punished perceived disloyalty and made the reporting of unwelcome information dangerous. [2]

Warnings without an adequate response

The Soviet government did not lack warnings that Germany might attack. The difficulty lay in judging their reliability, their timing and their relationship to German deception and British interests. Stalin believed that Britain had an obvious incentive to bring Germany and the Soviet Union into conflict. He also understood that Germany faced the risks of fighting while Britain remained undefeated. Those considerations helped him discount information that should have carried greater weight. Explaining his reasoning does not make the outcome a blameless misunderstanding: authority was concentrated in a leader whose assumptions could restrict the response to accumulating evidence. [2] It would nevertheless be inaccurate to imagine the entire Soviet military apparatus waiting motionless for permission to acknowledge reality. Units moved; reserves were called up under limited arrangements; commanders took precautions of differing scope. Naval readiness and the situation in individual districts did not follow one uniform pattern. The crucial question is what precautions were completed before the attack and whether they supported coordinated action. A defensive measure that left units dispersed or in transit might improve their prospects against a particular air raid while complicating the immediate concentration required for a counterattack. Readiness was a set of practical conditions, not a switch that could be thrown from the Kremlin. [2] The late-night directive associated with 21–22 June captured the tension. It warned of a possible attack, called for combat readiness and measures including the dispersal and concealment of aircraft, but also insisted that forces avoid provocations. Its transmission came too late to give all formations a common period in which to prepare. Commanders had to interpret urgent instructions through communications networks that were about to come under attack. A message received at an army or district headquarters was not simultaneously understood by every regiment, airfield and frontier post. [2]

A command distinction

Stalin was powerful before he held every wartime title

On the eve of invasion, Semyon Timoshenko was defence commissar and Georgy Zhukov chief of the General Staff. Stalin’s political authority was decisive, but the wartime Stavka had not yet been established. It would be created on 23 June with Timoshenko as chairman. Calling Stalin “supreme commander” in every formal sense on 21 June projects later appointments backwards. [6]

The uncertainty imposed an additional burden on lower commanders. They could see suspicious activity, hear reports and prepare locally, yet still lack authority for the scale of response the danger warranted. Once the invasion began, some of those same officers would be ordered to attack aggressively with incomplete knowledge of their own formations. The transition from excessive caution to unrealistic offensive demands was not a contradiction in the system’s political logic. Both placed obedience to central assumptions above the difficult business of establishing what was happening on the ground.

The coalition and the supply problem

Finland and Romania entered German planning for different reasons and under different arrangements. Finland sought to reverse losses imposed after the Winter War and increasingly cooperated militarily with Germany; Romania sought the recovery of Bessarabia and northern Bukovina, taken by the Soviet Union in 1940. Directive 21 anticipated the participation of both, but their forces were not simply additional German divisions. National command structures, territorial objectives and political calculations remained important. German operations from Finnish territory and the presence of German formations in Romania made cooperation materially significant before every formal declaration or major ground offensive had occurred. [4] The northern theatre in particular demands a separate clock. Operations from northern Finland towards Murmansk and the railway serving it were not identical to Army Group North’s advance from East Prussia. Distance, limited roads and difficult terrain constrained what could be accomplished there. The Soviet air attacks on Finland on 25 June and the Finnish government’s response would become important public markers of the Continuation War, but they should not erase the military cooperation already established. Conversely, Finland’s participation should not be described by simply transplanting the timing of German attacks in Lithuania onto the Karelian front. [3] Behind every sector lay the question of supply. German armies depended on railways for the large-scale movement of fuel, ammunition, food and replacements. Moving into the Soviet system required more than changing track gauge: bridges, locomotives, signalling, stations and damaged facilities affected the amount that could actually be delivered. Trucks extended the connection between railheads and fighting formations, but longer journeys consumed more fuel and vehicle life. Seizing a bridge intact was therefore valuable twice over, both for the immediate advance and for the maintenance of forces beyond it. [3] The popular picture of an entirely motorized German army is particularly misleading in this setting. The armoured and motorized formations formed a striking minority inside an army whose infantry usually marched and whose transport included enormous numbers of horses. Ziemke and Bauer give approximately 600,000 motor vehicles and 625,000 horses for the initial Barbarossa force; the figures describe the mixed character of the whole undertaking, not a uniform allowance per division. A mobile spearhead could move far ahead while the men required to secure its flanks and reduce pockets were still approaching on foot. That separation would become one of the campaign’s recurring operational problems. [2]

The orders behind the front line

Before the invasion, German authorities had also altered the conditions under which soldiers were to treat civilians and prisoners. The decree of 13 May on military jurisdiction in the Barbarossa area restricted the normal prosecution of offences against civilians and authorized violent measures against alleged resistance. Its importance lies in the institutional permission it supplied. It lowered restraints before the army encountered the population, allowing military authorities to treat whole communities through the categories of danger and reprisal. The document and its later examination at Nuremberg demonstrate that this was preparatory policy, not merely a spontaneous reaction to partisan warfare encountered during the advance. [7] The Commissar Order of 6 June went further by directing the separation and killing of captured Soviet political commissars. It expressly denied them the protection normally associated with prisoners of war. The order’s ideological language treated political identity as a reason for execution, turning capture into an occasion for selection and murder. Its existence prevents a separation of Barbarossa into a supposedly conventional military campaign followed by an unrelated SS war. The army’s own preparations included instructions for criminal treatment of particular captives. [8]

What the documents establish

Preparation does not require hindsight

The May jurisdiction decree and June Commissar Order existed before the border was crossed. They do not prove that every later atrocity followed an identical local process, but they establish that the removal of restraints and the killing of specified prisoners were built into the invasion’s preparation. Particular crimes still require their own evidence of date, place and perpetrator. [7] [8]

These measures also shaped what German victory would mean to those who survived the battles. The collapse of a Soviet headquarters might leave thousands of men without orders, but their danger did not end when they laid down their weapons. For civilians, an advancing formation could bring requisition, arbitrary punishment and the arrival of security units behind it. The military and social histories were therefore connected from the beginning. A road secured for supply was also a route along which occupation institutions could move; a prisoner column recorded as evidence of success consisted of people whose legal and physical protection had already been deliberately weakened. By the last hours of 21 June, Germany had assembled a force capable of inflicting an immense defeat on the Soviet armies near the frontier. It had not demonstrated that such a defeat would end the war. The Soviet leadership, meanwhile, had failed to convert its warnings and resources into an adequate response at the moment that mattered. Those two failures of judgment were not symmetrical: one accompanied an aggressive war of conquest, the other exposed a population and army to it. Before dawn, the distinction between plans and performance would cease to be theoretical. The opening assault would reveal both the extraordinary power of the German operational system and the first limits of what surprise could achieve.

German situation maps and staff reports are evidence of what German headquarters recorded, not an omniscient picture of the battlefield. Orders establish intentions; they do not by themselves prove execution. Postwar military accounts are checked against dated records and identified as retrospective. Place names follow familiar historical usage, with present-day equivalents where useful.
